title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
author: Andy Kroll
content:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the
Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical
activist ideology” and precipitated the planned departure of Smithsonian
secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the
culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on
Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming
midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia
suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent
in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal
Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and
dispatched them to ProPublica.

* * *

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the
history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several
million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If
implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an
unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is
structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea
Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new
permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”
and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new
“Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the
museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by
back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring
signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture”
on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s decision to retire
as head of the Smithsonian at the end of the year, the warning signs have yet
to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind
for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new
interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a
diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for
traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside
Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third
parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the
museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with
patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming
US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled
something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders
OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had
scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They
included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions
policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great
deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that
followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber
crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues
including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on
his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to
narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he
would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate,
carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He
disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee
checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the
Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who
previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected
last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The
Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month,
declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has
a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and
comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party
and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on
the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1
billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it
seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as
private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald
Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last
year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The
institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

![An aerial photo of three large museum buildings in Washington,
D.C.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2289386768_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Three
Smithsonian museums, dedicated to African American history, American history,
and natural history, seen from the Washington Monument Andrew Harnik/Getty
Images

As [recounted by ProPublica in
September](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-smithsonian-museum-american-
history-became-target-trump-culture-war), the American history museum has
faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled
with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in
2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to
produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the
national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian
underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in
Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-
reckoning.

By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of
fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent
exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved
members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks.
And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a
Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly
transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy,
hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and
artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or
representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights
on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was
failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that
it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated,
“including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the
development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the
nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this
front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.
